paras: The lynching of Bob Williams was the hanging of a Black man, also reported as Robert Williams, by a crowd of about one hundred men in the woods across the Saluda River from Pelzer, South Carolina, on November 4, 1881. Williams was accused of raping a nine-year-old white girl and was taken from the guard house at Williamston. A coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties, though a dispatch said the lynchers did not hide their identity and the lynching was "highly commended."

According to a Greenville News dispatch from Pelzer, the girl, an orphan named Blayton and ward of the Rev. Mr. Attaway of Williamston, was assaulted in a cotton field near Reedy River, and Williams threatened to cut her throat if she told. The Charleston News and Courier's Williamston correspondent instead called her a preacher's niece living with a Mr. Clark near Greenville. Williams was described as a field hand of about twenty to twenty-two, formerly of Greenville, said to have a wife and two children.

The News and Courier correspondent wrote that the girl's uncle and a neighbor seized Williams in his bed on the night of November 3 and lodged him in the Williamston guardhouse. By his captors' account, Williams repeatedly said he was guilty and begged to be shot. At eight o'clock about one hundred men gathered at the depot, had the girl identify him, and decided to take him back into Greenville County.

The crowd, "probably one hundred men of both colors" from Anderson and Greenville, marched Williams from the guard house through Pelzer about eleven o'clock. He reportedly confessed to a Black man and was granted a preacher. On a wooded hillside across the river he was set on a horse under a tree, and about noon the horse was driven from under him; the crowd left the body hanging.

Afterward, the same correspondent reported, an unnamed Black man said he would not have let the dead man be killed for that offense had he been kin. Members of the crowd put a rope around his neck, but "President Smythe" and a Mr. Caughfin interceded, and he was released on his promise never again to be seen in Anderson County.

Trial Justice Hawthorne came from Greenville that night and found the body still hanging. A jury with S. T. Hammond as foreman examined no witnesses and returned a verdict of death by hanging at the hands of unknown parties. Black residents reportedly refused to go near the body, and white men prepared to bury it on the hillside, though Williams had asked for burial at Greenville. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

Outside South Carolina the lynching circulated as a one-sentence Charleston wire item saying that a "negro named Bob Williams" had been lynched for an outrage upon a little white girl and had confessed. Papers in Minnesota, Memphis and Cheyenne printed it on November 6, and Tennessee, Mississippi and Arizona papers within a week. The Memphis Daily Appeal headed it "They Let Him Off Easy," while garbled briefs had a "mounted mob" take Williams from a house at night or placed the lynchers in "Greenwood."

The fuller accounts approved: the Chicago Tribune printed the Greenville version as "A Wretch Lynched in South Carolina," calling Williams a "black fiend." The News and Courier letter, reprinted in the Savannah Morning News, said the crowd gathered "to do justice" and called Williams "a demon too flendish to be buried" among human beings. South Carolina weeklies reprinted the Greenville News account; the Yorkville Enquirer headed it "Rape and Summary Punishment" and, like the Keowee Courier, kept a line about the dead man's "deceitful smile." The Newberry Herald noted only that he was hanged "in the daytime and publicly."

The two local correspondents, writing on the day, agree on a morning removal from the guard house and a noon hanging; the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer said he was taken from a house at night. The girl was "Blayton" in the Greenville News text and "Bessie Bladen" in the Yorkville Enquirer. The Chicago Tribune dispatch said "the little girl died late tonight," while the Keowee Courier and the Abbeville Press and Banner said she was in precarious condition after an operation.

reader.title: Lynching of Bob Williams
bases: A crowd of about one hundred men took Williams from the Williamston guard house and hanged him in the woods across the Saluda from Pelzer (A4, A7, A13).

Williams was hanged by a crowd of about one hundred men with no lawful authority, and a coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties (A4, A9, A13). The crowd acted to punish an accused rape of a white child, which the News and Courier letter called doing 'justice' (A7).

Two separate local correspondents, the Greenville News writer at Pelzer and the News and Courier writer at Williamston, agree on the seizure from the guard house and the hanging across the Saluda (A13, A7), and the Charleston wire confirms the lynching (A2).

accounts.gist: Williams was arrested at night, identified by the child at Williamston, taken from the guard house by about 100 men of both colors, confessed to a Black man, and was hanged in the woods across the Saluda about noon in a 'quiet and business' manner.

accounts.label: News and Courier correspondent at Williamston
accounts.gist: The girl's uncle and a neighbor arrested Williams and lodged him in the guardhouse; a crowd of about 100 at the depot decided to take him back to Greenville County and hanged him on the hill opposite Pelzer; a second Black man was nearly hanged afterward.

accounts.gist: A negro named Bob Williams was lynched in Greenville County for an outrage on a little white girl and confessed.

accounts.label: Lancaster variant

accounts.label: Coroner's jury

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News reprint called Williams 'a demon too flendish to be buried' and the crowd 'very orderly,' gathered 'to do justice' (A7).
The Chicago Tribune ran the South Carolina dispatch as 'A Wretch Lynched in South Carolina,' reporting the lynching 'highly commended' and Williams a 'black fiend' (A4).
The Yorkville Enquirer headed its account 'Rape and Summary Punishment' and kept a passage about the dead man's 'deceitful smile' (A15).
Most papers outside the state printed only the Charleston one-sentence item; the Memphis Daily Appeal headed it 'They Let Him Off Easy' (A2, A3).
The Newberry Herald stated briefly that he was hanged 'in the daytime and publicly' (A16).
